Issued at 1112 AM CST Sat Nov 14 2026

An upper level trough located near the Four Corners area will 
approach the Central/Southern Rockies over the next 24 hours. As
this upper level system approaches an area of low pressure will
develop along a surface boundary that will be located across 
Southeast Colorado/Northeast New Mexico and the Texas 
Panhandle. Increasing southerly flow ahead of this approaching 
upper wave will continue to draw Gulf moisture northward over 
this surface boundary and across southwest Kansas. This will 
result in increasing chances for accumulating rain from late
today through early Sunday morning. The cloud cover and rain 
chances late today and Sunday will also limit any warmup 
potential across southwest Kansas which will result in a weekend
of unseasonably cool temperatures. These clouds and light to 
moderate rainfall will end from west to east on Sunday as this 
system exits into the Lower Mississippi Valley, As this system 
moves east of western Kansas an upper level ridge will then 
begin to build across the Rockies and into the Central Plains 
during the first half of the upcoming work week. This will 
result in a period of dry conditions along with a gradually 
warming trend and increasing southerly winds. During the last 
half of the of the work week the upper ridge will move east of 
the area as our next Pacific upper level trough crosses the 
Western United States and approaches western Kansas. This will 
bring our next chance for precipitation to southwest Kansas. 

Widespread accumulating rainfall possible from late today 
through Sunday morning. Isolated embedded thunderstorms possible
near the Oklahoma border.  Moisture and lift will continue to 
improve across southwest Kansas over the the next 24 to 36 hours
as an upper level trough moves from the four corners region and
into the Southern Plains/Panhandle of Texas. This will produce 
widespread beneficial rainfall across much of southwest and 
south central Kansas from evening through early Sunday morning 
given the moisture, isentropic lift and 850-700 moisture 
transport that will occur north of a surface boundary over the 
Texas Panhandle and head of the upper level trough across 
southwest Kansas. WPC and latest guidance continue to indicated 
that there is a >75% chance for rainfall to be greater than 0.2”
south of the Arkansas river with a 60-70% chance of greater 
than 0.1” north of the river to the I-70 corridor. Near the 
Oklahoma border where better lift will be present along with mid
level instability there is a 50-70% chance for rainfall totals 
to be greater than 0.5”. Currently the best chance for the 
steadier and heavier rainfall to occur overnight will be near 
the Oklahoma border based on the moisture and isentropic lift 
north of a surface boundary that will be improving under 
improving difluent flow aloft. In addition to this improving 
lift there will be steepening mid level lapse rates that will 
accompany the upper level trough in this area which may also 
result in isolated thunderstorms near the Oklahoma border 
overnight. Any storm that does develop overnight near the 
Oklahoma border will be capable of producing isolate moderate to
heavy rainfall. Another area that may also be favorable for the
higher rainfall totals from this event will be near the 500mb 
deformation zone northwest of the upper trough/low that the REFS
has remaining nearly stationary, mainly west of highway 83, 
from late today through Sunday.

Chilly and damp conditions on Sunday followed by areas of fog 
Sunday night. As the upper level trough crosses southwest Kansas
on Sunday the rain will gradually taper off from west to east. 
Cloudy skies however will linger through late day which will 
limit any warmup potential Sunday afternoon. As a result 
temperatures will struggle to warm much more than 8-10F from the
overnight lows...if that much. Currently this would yield 
temperatures Sunday afternoon mainly in mid 40s. Sunday night a 
southeast winds will fall back to less than 10 mph. These light 
southeasterly upslope flow combined with recent rainfall will 
create a favorable environment for temperatures to fall back 
quickly in the 30s with fog developing towards midnight. 

Windy conditions with a gradual warming trend can be expected 
through mid week. Ensembles today were in good agreement that 
following the exit of the weekend upper level trough into the 
Mississippi Valley, an amplified upper level ridge will build 
into the Rockies and Central Plains. As this upper ridge crosses
the Plains early in the work week our next upper level trough 
will exit the eastern Pacific and begin to establish itself 
over the western United States. As the upper ridge builds east 
across the Rockies the westerly flow will improve which will 
result in falling pressures along the lee of the Rockies along 
with warming 850mb temperatures. A tight surface pressure
